document_sections.heading: 7. LOW SEXUAL DESIRE AND MALE HYPOACTIVE SEXUAL DESIRE DISORDER
document_sections.content: This section addresses the definition, contributing factors, assessment and management of low sexual desire in men.

document_sections.heading: 7.1 Definition, classification and epidemiology
document_sections.content: Sexual desire is difficult to define because it has several dimensions. Under International Classification of Diseases 10th edition (ICD-10), absent or diminished desire must be the main problem rather than a secondary feature of another sexual difficulty, such as ED. DSM-V describes male HSDD as a persistent or recurring lack of sexual or erotic thoughts, fantasies and desire for sexual activity; the clinician judges whether desire is deficient in light of age and the person's general and sociocultural circumstances. The fourth International Consultation on Sexual Medicine (ICSM) proposed a comparable definition as a clinical principle. The precise prevalence of LSD is unknown. A population survey of middle-aged German men (n = 12,646) reported a prevalence of 4.7%.

document_sections.heading: 7.2 Pathophysiology and risk factors
document_sections.content: Several causes may contribute to LSD. Levine described biological drive, psychological motivation and culturally shaped wish as components of desire, although these components are thought to overlap in both surveys and clinical care.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.1 Psychological aspects
document_sections.content: Negative thoughts during intercourse—including erection concerns, an absence of erotic thoughts and restrictive views of sexuality—predict LSD in men. Shame linked to such thoughts during sex distinguishes men with LSD from women with the same condition. Psychological symptoms arising during a crisis have also adversely affected male desire. Sexual satisfaction best explained dyadic desire in a cited study. Although LSD is less common in men than women, it is the most frequent concern in couples' therapy, making relationship factors important to address. A tendency toward anxiety is associated with LSD and is expected to divert attention from erotic cues toward worries. Approaches centred on differences in desire between partners, rather than identifying one partner as the problem, may reduce stigma and create opportunities for relationship-based management.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.2 Biological aspects
document_sections.content: Testosterone appears important for male desire, but circulating testosterone concentrations do not correspond directly to desire, particularly in older men. Table 7.1 identifies common biological and psychological causes. A possible contribution from thyroid and oxytocin hormones remains speculative.

document_sections.heading: Table 7.1: Common causes of low sexual desire in men [861, 870]
document_sections.content: The table lists common potential causes across endocrine, psychological, relationship, neurological, cardiovascular, renal, infectious and other sexual-health domains, as well as ageing and antidepressant therapy.

document_sections.heading: 7.2.3 Risk factors
document_sections.content: In the Global Study of Sexual Attitudes and Behaviours, which surveyed 13,882 women and 13,618 men across 29 countries, correlates of male LSD included ages 60-69 and 70-80 years, poor general health, vascular disease, current smoking, the belief that ageing diminishes sex, divorce in the past 3 years, financial difficulties in the last 3 years, major depression, concern about a relationship's future and fewer than one sexual relation per week. A study of middle-aged German men associated PE, ED and lower urinary tract symptoms with LSD. In that study, men with more than two children, more frequent solitary masturbation, greater perceived importance of sexuality or higher sexual selfesteem were less likely to report LSD.

document_sections.heading: 7.3 Diagnostic work-up
document_sections.content: Assessment encompasses components of desire, medical and sexual history, psychological and relationship concerns, and investigation when endocrine symptoms are present.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.1 Assessment questionnaires
document_sections.content: Sexual Desire Inventory (SDI) assesses influences on the development and expression of desire. Its self-administered 14 questions examine the intensity, frequency and personal significance of desire for partnered and solitary sexual activity. It distinguishes dyadic desire, involving sexual engagement, sharing or intimacy with another person, from solitary desire, involving sexual behaviour alone, potentially without interpersonal intimacy.

document_sections.heading: 7.3.2 Physical examination and investigations
document_sections.content: Men reporting LSD require a comprehensive medical and sexual history. Assessment should cover depressive symptoms and relationship difficulties, including partner conflict. If accompanying symptoms suggest an endocrine disorder, circulating total testosterone, prolactin and thyroid hormone concentrations can be assessed.

document_sections.heading: 7.4 Disease management
document_sections.content: Management of LSD should reflect its underlying cause.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.1 Psychological intervention
document_sections.content: Evidence for the efficacy of psychological interventions in LSD is sparse, so recommendations require caution. Cognitive and behavioural approaches may help men with LSD, and mindfulness-based treatment may also be promising. Because age-related sexual changes can affect both partners at the same time and influence each other, addressing an ageing couple's sexual-health needs together may be useful. Desire differences between partners can be a normal feature of relationships over the lifespan. Interventions directed at couples distressed by such differences avoid treating one partner as the sole source of the problem and may be less stigmatising.

document_sections.heading: Figure 7.1: Flow-diagram of psychological evaluation of patients with low sexual desire
document_sections.content: The figure outlines assessment of psychosexual history and development, the partner's role, dysfunctional thoughts and expectations about sexuality and male performance, whether diminished desire is dyadic or solitary, and particular anxiety triggers. These findings inform a decision about referral for sexual psychotherapy or another psychological intervention.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.2 Pharmacotherapy
document_sections.content: LSD associated with low testosterone can be treated using testosterone formulations, with treatment aimed at the physiological testosterone range. A meta-analysis found favourable effects of testosterone therapy on sexual motivation and sexual thoughts. Hyperprolactinaemia can cause LSD; prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas are an important cause, can be identified with pituitary MRI and can be treated with dopamine agonist agents. Accompanying hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism and diabetes should receive appropriate treatment. Major depression may be treated pharmacologically, but antidepressants can impair sexual functioning, so compounds with less effect on sexual function should be selected. Psychotherapy may improve the efficacy of pharmacotherapy, especially when depression underlies LSD.

document_sections.heading: 7.5 Recommendations for the treatment of low sexual desire
document_sections.content: Diagnose and classify LSD using medical and sexual history, potentially including validated questionnaires (Weak). Include physical examination in the initial evaluation to identify anatomical findings associated with LSD or other sexual dysfunctions, particularly erectile dysfunction (Weak). Perform laboratory investigations to exclude endocrine disorders (Strong). Adjust chronic treatments that can adversely affect desire (Weak). Provide testosterone therapy when LSD occurs with signs and symptoms of testosterone deficiency (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 8. PENILE CURVATURE
document_sections.content: This section addresses congenital penile curvature and Peyronie’s disease, including their evaluation and treatment.

document_sections.heading: 8.1 Congenital penile curvature
document_sections.content: Congenital penile curvature (CPC) is considered separately from Peyronie’s disease.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.1 Epidemiology/aetiology/pathophysiology
document_sections.content: CPC is rare, with a reported incidence of < 1%, although studies excluding hypospadias have reported prevalence of 4-10%. It results from unequal development of the corporal tunica albuginea and is not linked to urethral malformation. Curvature is usually ventral, may be lateral and is less often dorsal.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.2 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Medical and sexual history is generally sufficient to diagnose CPC. Patients commonly present after puberty, when erections and sexual activity make the curvature more evident; severe curvature can hinder or prevent intercourse. Physical examination and photographs during erection, preferably following intracavernous injection [ICI] of vasoactive drugs, are mandatory to document curvature and exclude other conditions.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.3 Disease management
document_sections.content: Surgery is definitive treatment and can be postponed until after puberty. A survey associated untreated ventral curvature with greater dissatisfaction about penile appearance, more intercourse difficulties and psychological problems; although these findings support correction during childhood, childhood surgery should be discouraged because penile growth is not complete. Described operations include plication techniques such as Nesbit, 16-dot, Yachia and Essed-Schröeder, with or without medial or lateral neurovascular bundle elevation and complete penile degloving. Corporal de-rotation approaches for ventral curvature have also been described, with reportedly minimal narrowing and shortening. No direct comparative studies establish a preferred operation.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.4 Summary of evidence and recommendation for diagnosis and treatment of congenital penile curvature
document_sections.content: The evidence summary states that medical and sexual history usually establish CPC, while examination and erection photographs, preferably after ICI of vasoactive drugs, are mandatory to document curvature (LE 3). It identifies surgery as the only treatment, to be deferred until after puberty and available during adult life when intercourse is significantly impaired (LE 3). Use the Nesbit procedure or plication, with or without medial or lateral neurovascular bundle dissection, to achieve satisfactory correction (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 8.2 Peyronie’s Disease
document_sections.content: Aetiology, risk factors and pathophysiology of Peyronie’s disease (PD) are addressed in Appendix 4 of the online supplementary evidence.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.1 Epidemiology
document_sections.content: Epidemiological evidence for PD is limited. Reported prevalence ranges from 0.4-20.3%, with higher prevalence among people with ED or diabetes. A USA survey estimated prevalence of definitive cases at 0.7% and probable cases at 11%, suggesting underdiagnosis. Onset commonly occurs at 50-60 years, but PD also affects men aged < 40 years, among whom reported prevalence is 1.5-16.9%.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.2 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Initial assessment establishes symptoms and their duration, including erection-related pain, palpable nodules, deformity, penile length and girth, and erectile function. It also addresses distress and risk factors for ED and PD. Peyronie’s disease questionnaire [PDQ] measures psychological and physical symptoms, penile pain and symptom bother. A focused history distinguishes active from stable disease to guide medical treatment and surgical timing: shorter symptom duration, erection pain or a recent change in deformity suggests continuing activity. Pain resolution and unchanged curvature for at least three months are accepted markers of stability and support referral for specific medical treatment or surgery when indicated. Examination begins with the genitals and extends to hands and feet for Dupuytren’s contracture or Ledderhosen plantar-fascia scarring. Assess palpable penile nodules or plaques; plaque size does not correlate with curvature severity. Measure stretched or erect penile length because it can affect treatment decisions and have medico-legal implications. Curvature must be assessed objectively during erection, through preferably home photographs of a natural erection, a vacuum-assisted erection test or ICI with vasoactive agents. ICI has been suggested to provide a superior assessment by producing an erection comparable to or stronger than one during sexual arousal. Computed tomography and MRI have limited diagnostic roles and are not recommended routinely. Erectile function may be assessed with IIEF, although it is not validated for PD. ED occurs in 30-70.6% of patients with PD; ED and psychological factors may substantially influence treatment choice. Ultrasound does not measure plaque size accurately but may help establish plaque presence, calcification and location. Doppler US may assess penile haemodynamics and the cause of ED, particularly arterial inflow before an intervention such as plaque incision and grafting to exclude arteriogenic ED.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.2.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for diagnosis of Peyronie’s disease
document_sections.content: Ultrasound plaque-size measurement is inaccurate and operator-dependent (LE 3). Doppler US may evaluate penile haemodynamics and vascular anatomy (LE 2a). ICI provides a superior objective assessment of erect curvature compared with other methods (LE 4). Obtain a medical and sexual history covering disease duration, erection pain, deformity, difficulty with vaginal or anal intromission and ED (Strong). Examine plaques, stretched or erect length, curvature using photography or induced erection, and related disorders such as Dupuytren’s contracture or Ledderhose disease (Strong). Use ICI for objective assessment of erect curvature during diagnostic evaluation (Weak). Use the PD-specific questionnaire particularly in trials; routine clinical use is not required (Weak). Do not routinely use US, computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging to assess plaque size and deformity (Weak). Use penile Doppler US when investigating ED to assess haemodynamics, vascular anatomy, and plaque location and calcification, particularly before surgery (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3 Disease management
document_sections.content: Management includes conservative options, mainly in earlier disease, and surgery selected according to disease stability, deformity, erectile function and patient circumstances.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3.1 Conservative treatment
document_sections.content: Conservative care primarily targets early PD as an adjunct to relieve pain and prevent progression, or patients who decline other treatments during the active phase. Proposed approaches include oral drugs, intralesional injections, shockwave therapy (SWT) and topical treatments. Study results frequently conflict, limiting practical recommendations. The Guidelines does not recommend oral pentoxifylline, vitamin E, tamoxifen, procarbazine, potassium para-aminobenzoate (potaba), omega-3 fatty acids or vitamin E combined with L-carnitine because efficacy has not been established. Limitations of the cited studies include lack of controls, small treated populations, brief follow-up and differing outcome measures. Even without adverse effects, these treatments may postpone more effective care.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3.1.1 Oral treatment
document_sections.content: The oral-treatment discussion considers Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors and Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

document_sections.heading: Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors
document_sections.content: Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors were proposed for PD in 2003 to reduce collagen deposition and increase apoptosis through inhibition of transforming growth factor (TGF)-b1. A retrospective study of 65 men suggested that tadalafil reduced curvature and remodelled septal scars compared with controls. In another study, 39 patients received vitamin E (400 IU) or sildenafil 50 mg for twelve weeks; pain and IIEF outcomes were significantly better with sildenafil. An observational retrospective study in acute PD with ED compared Tadalafil 5 mg once daily against no daily treatment (108 intervention vs. 83 controls). Curvature progression at 12 weeks was 25.9% vs. 39.7%, p = 0.042, respectively. Mean SHIM, PDQ-Overall and PDQPenile Pain scores improved significantly in the intervention group (p < 0.001).

document_sections.heading: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
document_sections.content: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may be offered for penile pain during active PD. Pain should be reassessed periodically while evaluating treatment effect.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3.1.2 Intralesional treatment
document_sections.content: Injecting an active agent into a penile plaque offers local delivery and higher concentrations within the plaque. Reliable delivery to the intended site can nevertheless be difficult, especially with dense or calcified plaques.

document_sections.heading: Calcium channel antagonists: verapamil and nicardipine
document_sections.content: The proposed basis for injecting channel antagonists derives from in vitro work. Published dosing schedules differ and findings conflict. Evidence is insufficient to support clinical use of injected verapamil or nicardipine; available results do not show a meaningful curvature improvement against placebo, and most studies did not compare groups directly with statistical testing.

document_sections.heading: Collagenase of Clostridium histolyticum
document_sections.content: Collagenase of Clostridium histolyticum (CCH) is a purified bacterial enzyme that selectively acts on collagen, the main constituent of PD plaques. Intralesional use dates to 1985. In 2014, EMA approved it for nonsurgical treatment of stable PD with palpable dorsal plaques, curvature of 30-90o and plaques that were not ventrally located. Administration requires a healthcare professional trained and experienced in its use. Its manufacturer has since withdrawn CCH from the European market, but the Guidelines retains its evidence and recommendations for completeness. The original study protocol used two 0.58 mg injections 24-72 hours apart every 6 weeks, for up to four cycles. IMPRESS II and II and post-approval studies evaluated efficacy and safety. Average curvature improvement was 34% with CCH versus 18.2% with placebo; three corporeal ruptures required surgical repair. Curvature between 30° and 60°, longer disease duration, IIEF > 17 and absent calcification were associated with the greatest likelihood of improvement. The placebo arm's 18.2% improvement from baseline raises questions about the contribution of injection and modelling independent of medication. IMPRESS I and II concluded that CCH improved physical and psychological aspects of PD. A post hoc meta-analysis found better results with curvature < 60o, onset > 2 years earlier, no plaque calcification and good erectile function. A proposed shortened protocol uses one 0.9 mg injection (one vial) per cycle along three lines around maximal curvature, for up to three cycles separated by 4-weekly intervals; home stretching, modelling and VED replace clinician modelling. Non-randomised studies reported results comparable to IMPRESS and apparent reductions in cost and treatment duration. A further prospective non-randomised multi-centre study examined this approach. In another large single-arm multi-centre study, longer PD duration, greater baseline PC and basal or dorsal plaque location predicted success. A nomogram likewise associated longer duration, greater starting curvature and basal plaques with greater likelihood of success, but requires external validation. Most recipients experienced at least one mild or moderate local adverse event: penile haematoma (50.2%), penile pain (33.5%), penile swelling (28.9%) or injection-site pain (24.1%). These events resolved spontaneously within 14 days of injection, and the adverse-reaction profile was similar across injections. Serious treatmentemergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 0.9% and included haematoma and corporeal rupture requiring surgery. IMPRESS and shortened-protocol data support advising against intercourse for the four weeks after injection to prevent serious TEAEs. Preliminary evidence suggests efficacy and safety during active disease. The document repeats these safety findings with different citations. It characterises CCH as an established treatment for stable disease while noting emerging evidence for an effect on progression during active disease. Controlled studies show a substantial traction or modelling effect, whereas modified-protocol studies generally have few participants and lack controls; patients therefore require full counselling about efficacy and high cost. It has been suggested that severe curvature might improve enough after CCH to permit plication rather than plaque incision and grafting, potentially avoiding the latter's greater adverse effect on erectile function, but further research must validate this possibility.

document_sections.heading: Interferon α-2b
document_sections.content: Compared with placebo, intralesional 5x10^6 units of IFN-α2b in 10 mL saline every 2 weeks over 12 weeks, for six injections in total, significantly improved curvature, plaque size and density, and pain; penile blood-flow measures also improved. IFN-α2b is described as effective regardless of plaque location and provides a > 20% curvature reduction in most men with PD. Reported mild adverse effects include sinusitis and flu-like symptoms; the latter can be treated effectively with NSAIDs before injection. Given the available moderately strong data and mild adverse effects, IFN-α2b is recommended for stable-phase PD.

document_sections.heading: Steroids, hyaluronic acid and botulinum toxin (botox)
document_sections.content: The sole single-blind placebo-controlled intralesional betamethasone study found no statistically significant change in deformity, plaque size or pain with erection. Reported adverse effects include tissue atrophy, skin thinning and immunosuppression. A non-randomised acute-PD study comparing intralesional hyaluronic acid with intralesional verapamil observed significant improvement in pain, curvature and IIEF-15. In an RCT, oral hyaluronic acid plus intralesional injection was superior to injection alone, with curvature improvement of 7.8±3.9 degrees and plaque-size reduction of 3.0 mm. Only one study has examined intralesional botox in men with PD, leaving insufficient evidence for clinical use.

document_sections.heading: Platelet Rich Plasma (PRP)
document_sections.content: Few human studies have assessed PRP effects on curvature, plaque size, PDQ or IIEF. Its effect in PD remains unproven and its use should be considered experimental. An ongoing phase 2b randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial enrolled 25 patients toward a planned 80 men with PD. Initial data from nine treated patients and eight placebo recipients showed no between-group difference in curvature at three months relative to baseline.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3.1.3 Topical treatments
document_sections.content: The topical-treatment discussion addresses verapamil and H-100 Gel.

document_sections.heading: Topical verapamil and H-100 Gel
document_sections.content: Evidence is insufficient that verapamil or H-100 Gel applied to the penile shaft, with or without iontophoresis, produces adequate active-compound concentrations in the tunica albuginea.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3.1.4 Other treatments
document_sections.content: Other approaches discussed include extracorporeal shockwaves, traction, vacuum devices and combined treatment.

document_sections.heading: Extracorporeal shockwave treatment
document_sections.content: The mechanism of ESWT in PD remains unclear. Four RCTs and one meta-analysis evaluated it: three trials used sham controls and one compared ESWT against ESWT plus PDE5I (tadalafil). All trials found pain relief, but none found improvement in curvature or plaque size. Eligibility criteria differed substantially and more research is needed. ESWT should therefore not be used as a primary treatment for curvature in PD.

document_sections.heading: Penile traction therapy
document_sections.content: Proposed mechanisms of penile traction therapy (PTT) include collagen remodelling through reduced myofibroblast activity and increased matrix metalloproteinase activity. Intended benefits are nonsurgical curvature reduction, greater girth and recovery of lost length. Evidence is limited by the small combined sample (267 in total), heterogeneous designs and non-standardised eligibility criteria; definitive conclusions cannot be drawn. Most studied patients still need further treatment to achieve curvature compatible with satisfactory intercourse. Effects in calcified plaques or hourglass and hinge deformities, theoretically less responsive, have not been studied systematically. Device use for 2-8 hours daily can be uncomfortable and inconvenient, although highly motivated patients have tolerated it. No serious adverse effects, including skin changes, ulcerations, hypo-aesthesia or reduced rigidity, were reported. PTT appears effective and safe, but evidence remains insufficient for a definitive recommendation as PD monotherapy.

document_sections.heading: Vacuum erection device
document_sections.content: Vacuum erection device (VED) therapy dilates cavernous sinuses, decreases retrograde venous flow and increases arterial inflow. Reported molecular changes include reductions in hypoxia-inducible factor-1α, TGF-β1, collagenase and apoptosis, alongside increases in endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) and α-smooth muscle actin. Only two retrospective studies have evaluated VED alone for mechanical straightening of PD curvature; further study is required.

document_sections.heading: Multimodal treatment
document_sections.content: Some evidence suggests combined oral drugs may treat acute PD, but there is no consensus on the drugs or optimal doses and no comparison among combinations. A long-term study reported efficacy for injectable verapamil with antioxidants and local diclofenac, including greater pain reduction than verapamil alone. Controlled trials have also examined combinations involving injections such as CCH; evidence on adjunctive PTT or VED is limited. Studies adding PTT to interferon, verapamil or CCH injections generally found no significant improvement in length or curvature, apart from a subset with a 0.4 cm length increase using devices for > 3 hours/day. In a meta-analysis, adjunctive PTT with surgery or injections increased mean stretched penile length (SPL) by 1 cm versus no adjunctive PTT, without a significant between-group curvature change. Reports of CCH with VED between injections found mean curvature improvement of -17o and length change of +0.4 cm after treatment; absent control groups prevent attribution of these effects to VED alone. Data suggest that sildenafil 25 mg twice daily after shortened-protocol CCH plus VED improves curvature and erectile function more than CCH alone, but external validation is needed.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3.1.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for conservative treatment of Peyronie’s disease
document_sections.content: The evidence summary places conservative care chiefly in early PD to relieve symptoms and limit progression (LE 3c). It finds no convincing support for oral acetyl esters of carnitine, vitamin E, potassium para-aminobenzoate (potaba) or pentoxifylline (LE 3c), and says oral tamoxifen is no longer recommended because of adverse effects (LE 3c). NSAIDs can address acute-phase pain (LE 4). Findings for injected verapamil and nicardipine conflict (LE 4). Intralesional Collagenase Clostridium histolyticum significantly reduced curvature and plaque diameter and length in stable PD (LE 1b); interferon may improve curvature, plaque characteristics and pain (LE 2b). Intralesional steroids have caused tissue atrophy, skin thinning and immunosuppression (LE 3c). The summary reports no high-level evidence supporting injected hyaluronic acid or botulinum toxin (LE 3c), while noting that injected hyaluronic acid may improve pain, curvature and IIEF scores (LE 2b) and that combined oral and injected hyaluronic acid improves curvature and plaque size (LE 1b). Evidence does not show adequate tunical concentrations after topical treatment (LE 3c), and efficacy data for iontophoresis are absent (LE 3c). Shockwave treatment may relieve pain without improving curvature or plaque size (LE 2b). PTT alone or with injections may improve curvature and length, but studies have major limitations (LE 3c). Offer conservative care when surgery is unsuitable or unacceptable (Strong), and explain all options and outcomes fully before treatment (Strong). Do not offer oral vitamin E, potassium para-aminobenzoate (potaba), tamoxifen, pentoxifylline, colchicine or acetyl esters of carnitine for PD (Strong). Use NSAIDs for acute-phase penile pain (Strong); use ESWT for that pain (Weak). Use phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors for concurrent ED or to optimise penetration when deformity makes intercourse difficult (Weak). Offer intralesional interferon alpha-2b for stable dorsal or lateral curvature > 30 degrees when a minimally invasive intervention is sought (Weak). Offer intralesional Collagenase Clostridium Histolyticum for stable PD with dorsal or lateral curvature > 30 degrees when nonsurgical treatment is requested, while acknowledging the high placebo effects (Strong). Do not inject steroids to reduce curvature, plaque size or pain (Strong). Do not use intralesional platelet-rich plasma or hyaluronic acid, alone or with oral therapy, for these outcomes outside a clinical trial (Strong). Do not offer ESWT to improve curvature or reduce plaques (Strong). Offer traction and vacuum devices to reduce deformity or within multimodal care, acknowledging limited outcome data (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3.2 Surgical treatment
document_sections.content: Conservative care may resolve painful erections in most men but produces substantial straightening in only a small proportion. Surgery seeks to correct curvature so penetrative intercourse is possible and is indicated for substantial deformity with intercourse difficulty and sexual bother. Disease should be stable for 3-6 months, or surgery should occur more than 9-12 months after PD onset. Once stable, failed conservative or medical treatment, extensive plaques or patient preference may also prompt surgery. Before reconstruction, document plaque size and position, curvature, hinge or hourglass deformity, penile length and ED status. Discuss intended benefits and risks to enable informed choice: shortening, ED, numbness, delayed orgasm, recurrent or residual curvature, palpable knots or stitches, possible circumcision and further penile wasting after shortening surgery. Procedure selection considers length, curvature and erectile function, including response to ED drugs, as well as expectations. Patients should understand that the primary aim is a functionally straight penis. Options comprise tunical shortening, tunical lengthening and penile prosthesis implantation, potentially with additional straightening for concurrent ED and residual curvature. Degloving with circumcision to prevent postoperative phimosis is described as the standard approach, although modifications exist; one study suggested circumcision may be unnecessary with a normal preoperative foreskin. Non-degloving approaches have been described to avoid ischaemic and lymphatic complications after subcoronal circumcision. No standardised questionnaire evaluates surgical outcomes. Prospective evidence is sparse and low-level; most outcomes come from retrospective, usually non-comparative and non-randomised single-centre studies or expert opinion, so they require caution.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3.2.1 Tunical shortening procedures
document_sections.content: Tunical shortening straightens the penis by reducing the longer convex side. It may suit men with good erections, adequate length, non-severe curvature and no hourglass or hinge narrowing. Techniques include excision, incision and plication. Nesbit excises an ellipse of tunica albuginea opposite maximal curvature. Yachia uses a longitudinal incision closed transversely under the Heinke-Mikowitz principle; Lemberger initially described the approach in 1984, and Yachia reported 10 cases in 1990. Pure plication places one or more folds without tunical incision or excision to limit potential veno-occlusive injury. The ’16-dot’ modification uses two parallel pairs of Essed-Schroeder plications, adjusted to curvature severity; results and satisfaction resemble incision or excision techniques. Across shortening techniques, complete straightening occurs in > 85%; recurrent curvature and hypo-aesthesia are uncommon (~10%), and postoperative ED risk is low. Shortening is the most frequently reported adverse outcome: 1-1.5 cm has been reported in 22-69% of patients. It rarely causes postoperative sexual dysfunction, although perceived loss can exceed measured loss. Measuring and recording penile length before and after straightening is therefore strongly advisable. The mainly retrospective studies do not adequately compare techniques, so evidence cannot establish a preferred method.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3.2.2 Tunical lengthening procedures
document_sections.content: Tunical lengthening entails incision or partial plaque excision on the concave side and graft coverage. Long-term length gain is uncommon; the goals are to limit shortening from plication and correct complex deformity. Additional plication or shortening is often required for residual curvature and may itself shorten the penis. Lengthening is preferable for marked shortening, severe curvature or hourglass or hinge deformity without underlying ED. Severe curvature has been proposed as > 60o, but that threshold lacks validation. An incision at maximal curvature, generally at the plaque, creates the grafted defect. Complete plaque excision may increase postoperative ED through venous leak, although partial excision may be permissible with substantial calcification. Patients without preoperative ED should be told postoperative ED risk can reach up to 50%. An ideal graft would resist traction, be manageable and flexible without excessive dilation, readily available, economical and minimally morbid; no material meets every criterion. Studies have not adequately compared graft types, so none can be singled out for recommendation. Egydio's geometric principles may guide incision site and graft dimensions. Grafts include autografts from dermis, vein, temporalis fascia, fascia lata, tunica vaginalis, tunica albuginea or buccal mucosa; deceased-donor pericardium, fascia lata or dura mater; animal-derived bovine pericardium, porcine small intestinal submucosa, bovine or porcine dermis, or TachoSil®; and synthetic Dacron® or Gore-Tex®. Autograft harvesting can cause complications. Dermal grafts have been associated with veno-occlusive ED (20%) and are absent from contemporary series. Vein grafts offer a theoretical endothelial-contact advantage; saphenous vein has been most commonly used, and extensive defects may need multiple incisions. Tunica albuginea grafts have suitable histology but limited harvestable size and potential effects on penile support and later prosthesis surgery. Tunica vaginalis is easily obtained and contracts little; a vascular flap may improve results. Buccal mucosal grafts have produced favourable short-term results under a proposed explanation involving nourishment and adherence of their submucosal surface. Cadaveric dura mater is no longer used because of infection concerns. Cadaveric pericardium (Tutoplast©) combines tensile strength with multidirectional elasticity/expansion by 30%; fascia lata and temporalis fascia offer stability and mechanical resistance. Porcine small intestinal submucosa (SIS) has been shown to promote regeneration, angiogenesis and host-cell development; bovine pericardium has favourable resistance, adaptability and tolerance. TachoSil© may shorten operating time, ease placement and aid haemostasis. Synthetic polyester (Dacron®) and polytetrafluoroethylene (Gore-Tex®) are generally advised against because of infection, inflammation and fibrosis, contraction and possible allergy. Proposed postoperative rehabilitation includes VED or PTT to prevent length loss of up to 1.5 cm. Daily nocturnal PDE5I can enhance nocturnal erections and graft perfusion and may reduce postoperative ED. Massage and stretching have also been recommended after wound healing.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3.2.3 Penile prosthesis
document_sections.content: Penile prosthesis (PP) implantation is generally reserved for PD with ED unresponsive to conventional drugs, including PDE5I or intracavernous vasoactive injections. Although inflatable prostheses (IPPs) have been regarded as more effective for ED generally, studies also support malleable devices with similar satisfaction in these patients. Available evidence suggests no meaningful difference among IPPs. Surgeons should advise on suitability, but patients should make the final device choice. Cylinder insertion alone usually gives excellent results for mild-to-moderate curvature. With residual intra-operative curvature < 30°, no additional correction is indicated because the device may straighten the penis over the following 6-9 months. If curvature is > 30°, first-line correction is modelling with the prosthesis fully inflated, bending opposite the curvature for 90 seconds, often with an audible crack. Persistent deviation > 30° may require incision, possibly with collagen fleece if coverage is needed, or plaque incision and grafting. Small defects may remain uncovered; grafting a larger defect can help prevent herniation, recurrent deformity or buckling as it scars. Overall complication risk is not higher than in the general population, although urethral perforation during modelling has been reported in 3%. In selected end-stage PD with ED and substantial shortening, simultaneous prosthesis insertion and length restoration has been proposed. The “sliding” technique is not recommended because glans necrosis has been reported after concurrent neurovascular-bundle and urethral release. MoST (Modified Sliding Technique), MUST (Multiple-Slit Technique) and MIT (Multiple-Incision Technique) have been described but should be restricted to experienced high-volume surgeons after thorough counselling. Satisfaction with IPP is significantly lower in PD than in the general IPP population; nevertheless, postoperative depression rates in PD decreased from 19.3%-10.9%. Because shortening is a leading cause of dissatisfaction after prosthesis implantation generally, patients with PD must be told that a prosthesis is not intended to restore their former penile length.

document_sections.heading: 8.2.3.2.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for surgical treatment of Peyronie’s disease
document_sections.content: The evidence summary limits PD surgery to stable disease with functional impairment (LE 2b). With concurrent ED unresponsive to medical treatment, prosthesis implantation with or without straightening is the preferred technique (LE 2a). Otherwise, length, erection rigidity, curvature, complex deformity and patient choice inform shortening versus lengthening (LE 3). Operate only after PD has remained stable for at least three months without pain or worsening deformity—usually after twelve months from symptom onset—and when deformity compromises intercourse (Strong). Before surgery, assess penile length, curvature, erectile function and ED-drug response, and expectations (Strong). Use tunical shortening first for CPC and for PD with adequate length and rigidity, less severe curvature and no hourglass or hinge deformity; surgeon and patient preference determines technique because none has proved superior (Weak). Use tunical lengthening for PD with normal erectile function and inadequate length, severe curvature or complex deformity; graft choice depends on surgeon and patient preference because no graft has proved superior (Weak). Do not use the sliding technique because of the significant risk of life-changing complications such as glans necrosis (Strong). Do not use synthetic grafts for PD reconstruction (Strong). Use a penile prosthesis, with or without modelling, plication, incision or excision and possible grafting, for PD with ED that does not respond to pharmacotherapy (Strong).

document_sections.heading: Figure 8.1: Treatment algorithm for Peyronie’s disease
document_sections.content: The algorithm starts with discussion of natural history, reassurance that PD does not cause malignancy, review of treatments and shared decision-making. Active disease is characterised by pain or worsening deformity or curvature; pain-control options shown are NSAIDs, tadalafil and LI-ESWT, with traction, intralesional CCH or IFN-α2b presented as optional. Stable disease lacks pain and deformity deterioration. For a patient seeking active treatment, erectile function and response to ED therapy guide subsequent choices. The diagram directs suitable patients with palpable dorsal, non-calcified plaques and dorsal curvature 30°-90° who cannot or do not want surgery toward intralesional CCH or interferon. Adequate length without severe curvature or complex deformity leads toward tunical shortening; a short penis, severe curvature or hourglass or hinge deformity leads toward tunical lengthening. ED unresponsive to treatment leads toward penile prosthesis. Residual curvature > 30° after prosthesis placement prompts manual modelling; persistent curvature > 30° then leads to tunical plication or plaque incision with grafting, whereas curvature < 30° requires no additional straightening.
